Step 1 showed one 401. Here are five, and why the caller matters. Every agent gets a passport. SPIFFE is the naming standard. SPIRE hands each agent a signed token, an SVID. Think of a sealed envelope with a passport inside, addressed to one recipient.

Look at the left. Five bad credentials, sent straight to the gateway, no model involved. All five got HTTP 401. The red row is a genuine SPIRE token, real signer, real name. It was only addressed to payments-mcp instead of the gateway. Refused.

Now the right. The caller is half the lookup key. Same rule: settlement-agent may pay up to its limit, the reviewer-ui may pay only a payment that is waiting for a human, and anyone else gets no row. "Identity is an input to the decision, not a label on it."

IF THERE IS TIME, run it live. No model call, no browser, costs nothing. From the repo root:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/e2e/test_policy_denial.py -v -k "criterion_4 or criterion_5"
SAY: "Criterion 4 is a walk over the source proving there is no policy logic in the settlement agent or the MCP server at all. Criterion 5 speaks MCP to the gateway directly with two different SPIRE-minted identities, and shows the verdict change with the caller."
Running it adds time; budget about a minute.

Source: Ch 7, Ch 14; aip-demo docs/demo-runbook.md §5 Beat 3

KASPER

Optional. Ring 1 · Reach has two layers, and William's demo shows one of them: Linkerd.

Plain words first. In his OSFF demo William used Linkerd, a service mesh: a small proxy beside every pod that checks the caller's identity at the destination's door. Our demo runs it too, for the way in. For the way out we use plain Kubernetes network policy, enforced in the node. The two do different jobs, and the choice came from a spike on 2026-10-12, on a separate cluster.

Left, Linkerd. Every attempt to go around the gateway, to payments-mcp or to the decision service, is refused with HTTP 403: a refusal you can read, where our old network layer gave silence. And the proxy counts every refusal, per policy. That held in the spike for pods with no proxy at all, and for pods told to skip it.

Right, network policy. Only the two agents with a model, settlement-agent and claims-agent, may reach the model provider, and they are allowed Anthropic's published address range, not the name. Linkerd's own egress rule couldn't do this job: it applies to a whole namespace, it matches only the server name the client claims, the SNI, and a pod that skips its proxy skips the rule. Network policy is enforced in the node, whether the pod cooperates or not.

SAY: "So reach has two layers: identity at the destination, and addresses in the node. Linkerd does the first; network policy does the second."

SAY, plainly, what we gave up against the old setup: "The model egress is now an address range, not a name. Any other host in that range is also reachable, and the range is Anthropic's to change. Between meshed pods, egress is decided per pod, not per port: a pod allowed to reach a peer's proxy (4143) can reach any port on that peer that listens on the pod IP; which ports answer is decided by the peer's Linkerd Servers, per port and per identity. And an egress drop is still silent: nothing answers and nothing counts it. Linkerd's refusals are loud: counted, and the proxy adds a span when the request carries a trace header."

SAY, before someone in the room does: "One caveat for a regulated audience: open-source Linkerd ships edge releases only. Its last open-source stable release was February 2024; stable builds now come from vendors."

IF ASKED about the trace: proxy tracing is on. The claim stays one trace, and the proxies add spans, four for each meshed hop: in the spike, 149 spans became 293. They are named by request path and carry no policy data. They put the mesh in the waterfall, nothing more. The control plane's own tracing stays off.

[verify: Linkerd edge-26.10.1 is the pinned release; the live run on Linkerd is still pending when this was written, so say "designed and measured in a spike", not "measured on this cluster"]

Source: Linkerd spike report, 2026-10-12 (criteria 1, 3, 4 and 6; the trace result; release channels); bounded-ai/README.md (Ring 1 · Reach)

The trace behind a held claim, the one you opened from the evidence, as Jaeger shows it. The slide shows the app's spans. Linkerd's proxies add their own, one per side of every meshed hop: in a held claim's trace we measured 148 of 313 spans from linkerd-proxy. Read it like the line under it says: indented means called by the line above, struck through means it never happened.

1. The root, northstar.claim.submit, carries the claim id. Under it the agent asks for execute_payment, and the gateway's tools/call carries jwt.sub, the caller's SPIFFE ID, and HTTP 200.
2. northstar.policy.decision: deny, €5,800 over the agent's limit of €0 at assisted. Its status is not ERROR. A refusal is the platform working; if it were an error, every dashboard you own would page you for correct behaviour.
3. Guardrail says gRPC status zero: the call to the decision service worked. That's how "the policy said no" stays different from "the policy service was down".
4. The struck-through lines: the gateway's call to payments-mcp, payments-mcp's execute_payment, and payments-api's execute. Never attempted.
SAY: "The execute never reached the tool. The absence is the evidence." The claim then waits for a person. The proposal and the refusal record are payments-api spans too, and they are there; what's missing is the execute. That only holds because we never sample.

[verify: the proxy-span count on the rehearsal's own trace]

Now we read what the bouncer writes down, for one permitted payment. Follow the rows down. First: tools/call, the request as it arrived. Twenty-two keys. jwt.sub is who asked, and gen_ai.tool.name is the only place the tool is named. Second: Guardrail, nine keys: the gateway phoning the policy service. grpc.status zero means the call worked, not what the answer was. Third: the policy service's span holds the why: rule, limit, amount. Fourth: the outbound call, six keys, and no jwt.sub, because the token was stripped. At the bottom: the four keys a refusal adds to span one. On a deny, span four doesn't exist.

Read the big number first. Two hundred is the HTTP status of the refused payment. The gateway marks its span ERROR with reason MCP, but the refusal travels inside a successful HTTP response: a tool result marked isError, with the rule, the limit and the amount in its text, ending in a short tag the agent reads. We probed it directly, with no model. A sealed envelope delivered on time, with a no inside. "Anyone alerting on HTTP status alone will not see this refusal at all." Metrics don't help. No agentgateway metric counts permit versus deny, and the Guardrail histogram counts every check, whatever the answer. In Northstar none of it reaches Prometheus anyway: nothing scrapes the gateway's port. The small line: from v1.6.0 the span carries the new attribute name. So alert on the decision span.

Before the detail, one idea: defence in depth. Think of airport security. You walk down a corridor, show your passport, go through the scanner, and meet the gate staff. No single check is trusted to catch everything. Each one assumes the one before it failed.

Next: the eight checks between an agent and a payment.

Source: Ch 7

KASPER

This is the question every platform team asks in an agent review: how do we limit what an agent can do with an MCP server? Here is Northstar's airport.

Read it from the top down. That is the order one tool call travels. Each row has three parts. On the left, the layer. In the middle, what it stops. On the right, what you would show an auditor as proof.

Rows two to four: who is calling, is the token real, is this call allowed. Row five: if the checker is down, the answer is no. Row eight: a human can overturn a refusal, but only by asking again as a different caller.

The one to remember is row one. Seven layers leave a span. The network doesn't. Its proof is BPF maps and TCP probes. A trace records what happened. Only network policy shows what couldn't happen.

Source: Ch 7

KASPER

There are two ways for the platform to say no. The gateway can do it alone, with one line of config: no payment over fifty thousand, for anyone. It answers 403 and says nothing else. The decision service is a service we wrote: it has the live dial, the rule's name, a reason the model can explain, and its own span. We use both. The gateway holds the hard ceiling; the service makes the decision.

Read the table top to bottom. Code to write: none against a service. Sees the tool's arguments: both, since agentgateway 1.6. Changes live: the gateway reloads its config in about a third of a second; the service reads a flag and nothing reloads. Says why: the gateway says "authorization failed" and nothing else; the service names the rule and the limit. In the trace: the gateway leaves one span; the service leaves northstar.policy.decision.

The line at the bottom is the real rule, from the config file. It is an allow rule on purpose: a deny rule lets a string amount through, and we measured that. The ceiling is not in the live demo. scripts/demo ceiling shows it if someone asks.

[verify: agentgateway is a Linux Foundation project hosted in AAIF, not CNCF.]

Source: docs/architecture.md "Two ways to say no"; tests/e2e/test_gateway_ceiling.py

The gateway has a second family of guardrails, for the model's own traffic. We read the list from the source, at the v1.6.0 tag. Regex rules mask or reject text. Personal data, like card numbers and emails, is found and masked. A moderation model can judge a prompt. A webhook lets your own service judge. And there are connectors for Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety and Google Model Armor.

SAY, plainly: "Northstar's model calls do not go through the gateway today. So none of these are in the demo." Routing them through the gateway is a separate piece of work.

KASPER

There are two ways for a platform to say no. William's demo shows one, Northstar shows the other. They're layers, not rivals.

On the left: hide. In William's OSFF demo the gateway has a static allowlist, one CEL line: the tool's name must be in this list. Anything else isn't there. Ask the gateway for its list of tools, and the forbidden one never appears. Call it anyway, and you get HTTP 400, Unknown tool. Think of a building where the vault isn't on the map. The agent can't even ask for it.

On the right: refuse and record. Our payment tool isn't hidden. You saw it in step 1: with the settlement agent's identity, tools/list shows all four tools, execute_payment included. Listed is not permitted: every call is decided. It can't be hidden, because paying claims is the agent's job. Whether a call is fine depends on its arguments: at autonomous the limit is six thousand: five thousand eight hundred, yes. Six thousand two hundred, no. At assisted the limit is zero, so even five thousand eight hundred waits for a person. So the call is proposed, refused, recorded as a northstar.policy.decision span with the rule and the limit, and explained, to the customer now and to an auditor later.

Use both. Hide what an agent must never touch. Refuse, and record, the rest. And credit where it's due: the hide layer, and the rings you've been seeing all along, are William's.

[verify: agentgateway 1.6.0 gives CEL the tool's arguments, so a gateway rule can now refuse by amount too (the previous slide). Hiding is still the cheaper layer, and refusing is still the one that leaves a record.]
[verify: William's demo ran agentgateway v1.3.1; the HTTP 400 Unknown tool and the tools/list filtering are from his README, checked against that version's source]

One more idea. In a power cut, what does the door lock do? Fail-closed: it stays locked. Fail-open: it swings open, like a fire exit. For a payment gate, only one of those is safe. So which does ours do?

Source: Ch 7

Last idea before the demo. On the left, a parent edge: inside one trace, the parent waits while its child runs. On the right, a span link: two separate traces, and a pointer back, like "see also". You use a link when someone took minutes, in another process.

KASPER

Maker and checker. The agent makes the payment. A human checks it. These are two traces, and the slide shows both.

1. Left, trace A: the maker. The agent proposes: the claim came in, the agent asked to execute the payment, and the platform said a person decides. The agent records "input required" and its work is done: trace A ends at the hand-off. Nothing polls while the claim waits, and nothing moved.
2. Right, trace B: the checker. A person approves it. The reviewer-ui records northstar.review.decision, asks the gateway to execute the payment under its own identity and its own rule, human-approved.execute, and then resumes the claim. The decision service has read the ledger and seen that the payment is waiting for a human, so it permits. When the claim completes, the platform pushes the outcome to the customer's page.
SAY: "Nothing was overridden. A different caller was asked about."
The empty middle is the point: human time. Minutes, maybe hours, and nothing runs or polls while the claim waits.
3. The dashed line is a span link: B's resume points back to A. A link, not a parent. "Work separated by human time is two traces and a link. Nothing polls while the claim waits." A parent edge would have misstated both the duration and what was executing.
4. The bottom line is a Prometheus question: how long do humans take? One histogram, by autonomy level and decision. The 95th percentile per level shows whether widening the band really cut the human's load.

Honest limits: Reject is final and the customer is told their claim was declined; but there is no second approver, no timeout, no expiry, and no login on the reviewer-ui. The reviewer id is a string the form supplies.

Source: aip-demo docs/demo-runbook.md §5 Beat 4; docs/telemetry-contract.md (trace B, northstar_approval_wait_duration_seconds); Ch 8

Optional. Step 3 flipped the value from the command line. Backstage, the developer portal, does the same write with a button, and that's the point: Backstage is only a view onto the same object.

1. Before: settlement-agent reads assisted, a live read of the Kubernetes object.
2. One click: settlement-agent reads autonomous.
3. The same €5,800 claim: settled by the agent, no human. At assisted it had waited for a person.
4. The difference from the CLI: Backstage's write path records one span per flip, northstar.autonomy_contract.change, with the previous and the new value. The CLI flip in step 3 leaves no such span.

Source: aip-demo docs/demo-runbook.md §5 Beat 7 (the longer version), §7; platform/backstage/packages/backend/src/plugins/autonomyContract/telemetry.ts

KASPER

"The platform API is the resource. kubectl and Backstage are just views a person uses to read and change it." And as step 4 showed, who may write it is enforced too. managedFields records who wrote a value last, but the next write wipes it, like a whiteboard. That's why Backstage writes one span per flip, which survives the revert and the pod. The CLI flip in step 3 writes none; the evidence for it is the claim's own northstar.policy.decision, which names the level it was decided under.
